Take 1 hour before or 2 hours after food on empty stomach
Use if benefit outweighs risk; give vitamin K near term
Compatible; small amounts in milk, monitor infant

summary: Rifampicin (rifampin) is a rifamycin antibiotic central to tuberculosis and leprosy therapy and used for meningococcal carrier eradication. It inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. It is a potent inducer of CYP enzymes causing extensive drug interactions, harmlessly turns body fluids orange-red, and can cause hepatotoxicity and flu-like reactions with intermittent dosing.
indications: Treatment of all forms of tuberculosis (in combination regimens)
Elimination of meningococci from the nasopharynx in asymptomatic Neisseria meningitidis carriers
Off-label: prosthetic-device and staphylococcal infections as adjunct; Haemophilus influenzae type b prophylaxis

dosage.d: 10 mg/kg once daily, not to exceed 600 mg/day (oral or IV)
dosage.n: Part of multidrug regimen (e.g., with INH, pyrazinamide)

dosage.d: 10-20 mg/kg once daily, not to exceed 600 mg/day
600 mg once monthly (WHO MDT) with dapsone +/- clofazimine

admin: Take oral rifampicin once daily on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal, with a full glass of water
For IV use, reconstitute and infuse per label; IV dose equals the oral dose
Give as part of an appropriate combination regimen for TB and leprosy to prevent resistance
Warn that urine, sweat, tears and other secretions turn orange-red and may stain soft contact lenses
Obtain cultures/susceptibility before therapy and monitor during treatment
moa: Rifampicin binds to and inhibits the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking RNA synthesis. It is bactericidal against Mycobacterium tuberculosis and many gram-positive and gram-negative organisms but does not inhibit the mammalian enzyme. Resistance arises rapidly through rpoB mutations, so it is used in combination.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to rifampicin or any rifamycin
Concurrent use with ritonavir-boosted saquinavir (severe hepatotoxicity)
Concurrent use with certain antivirals whose levels it markedly lowers (atazanavir, darunavir, fosamprenavir, saquinavir, tipranavir, cabotegravir, fostemsavir, lenacapavir)
monitor: Numerous CYP3A4/2C9/2C19 substrates (warfarin, oral contraceptives, many others)

preg: Crosses the placenta. Used in tuberculosis when the benefit outweighs the risk; isolated reports of fetal abnormalities. Administer vitamin K to mother and neonate when given in the last weeks of pregnancy to reduce postnatal hemorrhage risk.
lact: Small amounts are excreted in breast milk; generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Monitor the infant for jaundice and orange discoloration.
renal: Primarily eliminated by the liver/biliary route, so no major dose adjustment is needed in renal impairment, though caution is advised with doses above 600 mg/day.
hepatic: Can cause dose-related hepatotoxicity. Use cautiously and monitor LFTs in patients with liver disease, alcoholism, or on other hepatotoxic drugs; reduce dose or discontinue if significant hepatic injury occurs.

major: Many antiretrovirals and protease inhibitors - markedly reduced levels (several contraindicated)
Warfarin - reduced anticoagulant effect; INR monitoring and dose increase needed
Oral contraceptives - reduced efficacy; advise additional non-hormonal contraception
Other strong CYP3A4 substrates (e.g., many calcium-channel blockers, certain immunosuppressants like cyclosporine/tacrolimus) - reduced exposure
moderate: Sulfonylureas, corticosteroids, statins, azoles, phenytoin, digoxin - reduced exposure
minor: Antacids - reduced rifampicin absorption if taken together
interactions.food: Food reduces and delays absorption; take on an empty stomach (1 h before or 2 h after meals).
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive serum folate/B12 and abnormal LFTs; interferes with some bilirubin and BSP excretion tests; colors fluids orange-red.

common: Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, saliva (harmless)
GI upset - nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain
serious: Flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, myalgia) with intermittent or high-dose therapy
emergency: Severe immune-mediated reaction with hemolysis, thrombocytopenia or acute renal failure (stop drug, do not rechallenge)

monitoring: Baseline and periodic liver function tests, especially with risk factors
Renal function if immune reactions suspected
Bacteriologic cultures before and during therapy to confirm susceptibility/response
Review concomitant medications for CYP induction interactions
counsel: Take on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals
Expect harmless orange-red color of urine, sweat and tears; it may permanently stain soft contact lenses
Use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method while on rifampicin
Report yellowing of eyes/skin, dark urine, loss of appetite, fever or unusual bleeding
Do not skip doses and complete the full TB/leprosy course; tell all providers you take rifampicin
pk: Bactericidal within hours; clinical TB response over weeks
Store at 25 C; protect from light; avoid excessive heat
pearls: Potent inducer of CYP3A4 and other enzymes - the most interaction-prone TB drug; always review co-medications (warfarin, OCPs, antivirals, immunosuppressants)
Harmless orange-red discoloration of body fluids; warn about permanent staining of soft contact lenses
Flu-like syndrome, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and acute renal failure are immune reactions seen with intermittent/high-dose use - stop and do not rechallenge
Always use in combination to prevent rapid emergence of resistance (rpoB mutations)
US spelling 'rifampin' equals international 'rifampicin' - same drug
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; then skip it and resume the regular schedule. Do not double up. Consistent daily dosing is important to prevent TB resistance.
overdose: Acute overdose causes nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, pruritus, lethargy, and orange-red 'red man' discoloration of skin and fluids; hepatic enzyme rise and unconsciousness can occur with severe liver disease. Treat with gastric decontamination, supportive care and forced diuresis; bile-clearing measures and hemodialysis may help in severe cases.
